sugestoes.texto: On the Storage.Create error path the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`, recording a legacy-storage metric for a call that was made against the unified Storage. This mislabels storage failures as legacy failures, so any alerting/dashboard that distinguishes the two stores will report the wrong backend as failing. It should call `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`.

On the Storage.Update error path the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`, recording a legacy metric for a unified-Storage failure. This mislabels storage errors as legacy errors and corrupts the per-store error metrics. It should call `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

In the DeleteCollection async goroutine, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration`, not `recordLegacyDuration`. Every other legacy call in this file (and modes 1/2) records the legacy metric, so legacy delete-collection failures are attributed to the storage metric and never surfaced as legacy errors.

Delete builds an enriched logger with name/kind/method (`log := d.Log.WithValues(...)`) on line 96 but then stores `d.Log` (the un-enriched parent) into the context on line 97. All structured fields added to `log` are discarded, so Delete emits log lines without name/kind/method while every sibling method preserves them — making Delete failures hard to attribute. Use `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

Update's async legacy goroutine passes the original `objInfo` straight to `d.Legacy.Update`, dropping the previous `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` wrapping. Since `UpdatedObject` is re-invoked by the legacy store, legacy now recomputes its own updated object instead of persisting the exact object written to unified Storage, so the two stores can diverge — defeating the dual-write safety purpose. Wrap objInfo with the object returned from Storage.Update before calling the legacy store.

The async legacy Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection goroutines reuse the request `ctx` (e.g. line 51 `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` with ctx from the handler). The kubernetes apiserver cancels the request context as soon as the response is written, so this goroutine's Legacy call is cancelled almost immediately and the backup write never completes — the 'safe measure' legacy write silently does nothing on the fast path. Detach the context (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or a fresh background context with the 10s timeout) so the backup write can finish.

The Delete success path records `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing `name` (the object name) as the metric label where every other storage metric in this file passes `options.Kind`. This creates a high-cardinality, inconsistent label series (one per object name) that breaks aggregation with the other `method=delete` samples and can blow up metric cardinality. Pass `options.Kind` for consistency.

On the Storage.Create error path the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) using the storage start time. This records a storage failure in the legacy-duration histogram (metrics.go:54 writes m.legacy) while the storage histogram is never updated, so storage create errors are invisible on the storage metric and pollute the legacy metric. Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...) here.

On the Storage.Update error path the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) with the storage start time. This mislabels a storage failure as a legacy failure (metrics.go:54 vs :59), leaving the storage update error unrecorded in the storage histogram. Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...).

In the DeleteCollection async goroutine the legacy result is recorded with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy). This writes the legacy duration/outcome into the storage histogram (metrics.go:59) instead of the legacy one, so the legacy DeleteCollection latency is recorded under the wrong metric and the storage metric is polluted. Use d.recordLegacyDuration here.

Delete builds an enriched logger with name/kind/method (log := d.Log.WithValues(...)) but then stores d.Log (not log) into the context via klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log). The enriched logger is discarded, so all downstream logging for the delete path loses the name/kind/method fields. Pass `log` to klog.NewContext.

Update's async legacy goroutine passes the original objInfo straight to d.Legacy.Update, dropping the previous updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj} (dualwriter.go:128-144) that made legacy receive the object Storage actually persisted. Legacy now re-applies the caller's UpdatedObjectInfo against its own current object instead of the storage result, so the legacy write can persist a different object than the unified store (and diverge under forceAllowCreate). Rebuild the wrapper with the object returned by Storage.Update.

The async legacy goroutines reuse the request ctx (e.g. context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...) at lines 51, 110, 135, 163), so when the HTTP request finishes and its context is cancelled the legacy write is aborted immediately. This defeats the stated purpose of the fire-and-forget legacy write as a safety net, silently dropping dual-write data. Detach the goroutine from the request context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) plus the timeout).

Delete's success path calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage), passing `name` in the `kind` label position. The metric's kind dimension is populated with the object name, corrupting the storage-duration series for every delete. Pass options.Kind instead of name.

issues.descricao: Delete puts the base d.Log instead of the enriched per-call logger into the context, so downstream logs lose name/kind/method fields.
issues.textoGolden: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

comentarios.texto: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` installs the mode-level logger instead of the request-scoped `log` built on line 96 (which carries name, kind and method) — a copy/paste error, as every other method in this file passes the composed `log`. Storage.Delete and the legacy delete goroutine therefore log without the per-request fields this PR is adding (and without the metrics method/kind context).
ctx is built with klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of the enriched `log`. The delete logs then lose the name, kind and method values. Use `log`.
The Delete context uses d.Log rather than the per-call log. This is a logging-context inconsistency (not a data leak); use the per-call logger for consistency.

issues.descricao: The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine records its duration with recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, misattributing legacy latency and errors to the storage metric.
issues.textoGolden: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

comentarios.texto: The legacy DeleteCollection duration and error status are recorded in the unified-storage histogram. Every successful unified deletion therefore produces a second storage observation for a different backend, while legacy deletion failures are attributed to unified storage and no legacy observation is emitted. Call recordLegacyDuration here instead.

The timed call is d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, but its measurement is emitted using recordStorageDuration. Use recordLegacyDuration; otherwise storage receives two measurements for a successful collection deletion and legacy receives none, and legacy failures appear as storage failures.
The legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded with recordStorageDuration, so legacy latency and errors are attributed to storage. Use recordLegacyDuration.

issues.descricao: Delete's success path records the storage metric with the object name in the kind label instead of options.Kind, creating per-object series and inconsistent labels.
issues.textoGolden: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

comentarios.texto: The Delete success-path metric passes `name` where every other call site in this file (lines 48, 103, 113, 156, 159) passes options.Kind in the kind/name argument slot. The storage-success sample for Delete is thus labelled with the object name instead of the resource kind, breaking label consistency with the other operations and with the error sample emitted at line 103. Use options.Kind here (or insert name consistently everywhere, matching the metric's label semantics).
recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) at line 106 passes the object name in the kind label slot.

recordStorageDuration is called with the object `name` as the `kind` label: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. Every other storage call site passes `options.Kind` (lines 73, 89, 103, 156, 159). This injects a per-object value into the kind label, corrupting the metric and giving it unbounded cardinality (one series per object name), which grows memory on every delete. Should be `options.Kind`.

issues.descricao: On storage Create/Update failure the duration is recorded with recordLegacyDuration, attributing unified-store errors to the legacy metric.

comentarios.texto: On a Storage.Create failure the code records the error with recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) — the failing subsystem is Storage, not Legacy, and it passes the storage start time. This records storage failures under the legacy metric, corrupting the dual-writer error dashboards (and contradicts the success path on line 48 which uses recordStorageDuration). Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

On a Storage.Update failure the code records the error with recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), attributing a storage failure and its storage duration to the legacy metric. This is inconsistent with the success path on line 132 (recordStorageDuration) and with mode1's semantics. Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

The async goroutine performing the LEGACY DeleteCollection measures it with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). Every other legacy write in this file uses recordLegacyDuration (lines 56, 113, 140); recording it under the storage metric reports legacy latency/errors as storage latency/errors. Use d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy).

issues.descricao: Mode 3 legacy writes now run in background goroutines derived from the request context, which is cancelled when the request completes, so legacy writes can be cancelled and legacy storage falls out of sync.

comentarios.texto: The async legacy write goroutine derives its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)). The apiserver cancels that context as soon as the HTTP handler returns — which is immediately after Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection return — so the goroutine's Legacy.Create can be canceled before completing, silently dropping the legacy write that this mode exists to guarantee. The same applies to the goroutines at lines 108-114, 134-141 and 161-167. Detach the async context from request cancellation (e.g. derive from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) / context.Background()) before applying the timeout.

The legacy write in Mode 3 became fire-and-forget, changing the contract callers relied on: previously Create (and, identically, Update/Delete/DeleteCollection) returned only after the LegacyStorage call had been made in-request; now it returns immediately and the write runs in a detached goroutine. Worse, the goroutine builds its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (line 51: `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`), which the API server cancels as soon as the handler returns/flushes the response — so the legacy write and its 10s timeout will typically be cancelled outright and the legacy store silently stops being updated, which is precisely what the new mode-3 integration cases assume still happens. Any detached work must be given a context not tied to the request lifetime (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a server-lifetime context), and consumers that depended on the synchronous legacy write need to be updated.

The asynchronous legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context, which is canceled when the HTTP request finishes. Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection return before this work completes, so their legacy database operations can be canceled immediately instead of receiving the intended ten-second window. Derive the bounded background context from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) to retain request values without inheriting request cancellation.

issues.descricao: Legacy.Update now receives the original objInfo instead of a wrapper carrying the object stored in unified storage, so legacy recomputes the update and can diverge.

comentarios.texto: Legacy.Update receives the original objInfo instead of the object successfully committed to unified storage. The playlist legacy implementation calls objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old) against its own legacy object, so a patch is reapplied to potentially stale state and can persist a different result or fail rather than mirror the unified write. Pass an updateWrapper containing res, as the previous implementation did.

Legacy.Update previously received an updateWrapper containing the object returned by Storage.Update; it now receives the original objInfo. UpdatedObjectInfo can compute an update from the old object supplied by each backend (notably for patches), so evaluating it against a stale legacy object can produce a different result or reject an update that already succeeded in Storage. Preserve the canonical-result contract by passing an updateWrapper with updated: res and upstream: objInfo to the legacy consumer rather than replaying the original update against legacy state.

Legacy.Update now receives the original objInfo rather than the updateWrapper containing the object successfully committed to Storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can represent a patch/transform based on the supplied old object; replaying it against legacy's potentially different old state can persist a different result or fail, even though the authoritative update succeeded. Restore forwarding of the committed result via updateWrapper instead of recomputing the update against legacy state.

issues.descricao: The Mode 3 tests never wait for or assert the asynchronous legacy writes, and legacy and storage share one mock, so removing the legacy calls would not fail them.

comentarios.texto: The legacy half of Mode 3 is never verified, so these tests cannot catch its removal. Mode 3 is documented as writing to BOTH LegacyStorage and Storage, and the implementation performs the legacy write in a detached goroutine (`go func(){ d.Legacy.Create(...) }()`, dualwriter_mode3.go lines 50-57, and likewise at 108-114, 134-141, 161-167). Each test registers legacy expectations (`setupLegacyFn`, e.g. lines 30-32 and 40-42) but never calls `m.AssertExpectations(t)`, `AssertCalled` or `AssertNumberOfCalls`, and never waits for or observes the goroutine — no channel, no polling. Additionally `legacyStoreMock{m, l}` and `storageMock{m, s}` (lines 53-54, and the same pair in every other test function) share one `*mock.Mock`, so even a count assertion could not distinguish a legacy call from a storage call. Deleting every `d.Legacy.*` call from the implementation leaves all six tests passing, which is exactly the regression the names — and the Mode 3 contract — claim to cover.

The successful Create test never verifies the legacy write. Configuring m.On("Create", ...) does not require that expectation to be consumed, and these assertions only inspect the object returned by Storage.Create. Deleting the entire legacy-create goroutine would still pass this test. Use distinct storage and legacy mocks and synchronize on the legacy call, then assert that it completed with the intended object.

The successful Update case configures a legacy Update expectation but returns after checking only the unified-store result. It neither waits for the asynchronous legacy update nor verifies its expectation, so removing the legacy-update goroutine entirely still passes. Add explicit synchronization and verification of the legacy update (ideally with separate mocks), including the object propagated to legacy storage.

issues.descricao: The List error test case is still named 'not implemented' although List is now implemented and the case checks storage error propagation.

comentarios.texto: The test-case name "error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented" still describes the old stub List (which returned nil, nil with a "List not implemented" log). List is now implemented at dualwriter_mode3.go:79 and delegates to Storage.List; the case merely checks that a Storage error is propagated. The name contradicts the code it now exercises — rename it, e.g. "error when listing objects in the unified store fails".

issues.descricao: The Create test case name says 'only in the unified store' although Mode 3 also writes to legacy.

comentarios.texto: The test name says creation happens "only in the unified store", but this case configures a successful Legacy.Create as well, and Mode3.Create launches that legacy write after the unified write succeeds. Rename the case to describe creation in both stores (with the legacy write asynchronous), so test output does not communicate the opposite of the mode-3 write contract.

issues.descricao: Independent per-request goroutines remove ordering between legacy writes to the same resource, so legacy can end up with an older version or a resurrected object.

comentarios.texto: Independent goroutines remove ordering between successful writes to the same resource. For example, Storage commits update A and then update B, but the legacy goroutine for B can finish before A, leaving legacy with A while Storage contains B. Likewise a delete can run before an earlier create and leave a resurrected legacy object. Preserve per-resource commit order for mirroring (including across create/update/delete), rather than launching each write independently.

issues.descricao: The storage-failure Create test registers its failing expectation via setupLegacyFn and only works because legacy and storage share one mock.

comentarios.texto: The 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' case registers the failing Create expectation only through setupLegacyFn. It passes only because legacy and storage share one mock, so the storage Create gets that error by accident. Register the expectation in setupStorageFn and use separate mocks for legacy and storage, so the test really covers a storage failure.

issues.descricao: DualWriterMode3.Delete now returns on any unified-storage error, including NotFound, before deleting from legacy, so objects that exist only in legacy can no longer be deleted.
Mode 3 legacy-storage write errors (create/update/delete/delete-collection) are no longer logged after moving to async goroutines; only a duration metric with an error flag is recorded.

sugestoes.texto: When the shared credential endpoint is enabled, the parse uses minimumTokenResponseSchema, which defines no refresh_token key, so zod strips the key and `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token` is undefined; the assignment on line 26 mutates a key that was never part of the parsed schema and is dropped on the returned object. Callers such as zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:120 and webex/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:101 then read `newTokens.refresh_token` (undefined) and persist it, breaking the next refresh. Define refresh_token on minimumTokenResponseSchema (or return a normalized object) rather than assigning onto a stripped parse result.

The refresh response is rejected based on `response.statusText !== "OK"`, but Node's undici fetch frequently returns an empty statusText (HTTP/2 responses, many proxies), so valid 200 responses throw `HttpError(400)` and the Salesforce integration fails to authenticate. Check `response.ok` (or `response.status !== 200`) instead of the human-readable statusText.

parseRefreshTokenResponse throws when parsing fails, so `accessTokenParsed.success` is always true here and the guard on lines 92-94 is dead code; more importantly the helper returns the zod SafeParseReturnType, not the token object, so `...accessTokenParsed.data` is spread into the stored key and `accessToken`/`instance_url` expectations later in getClient come from the stale credentialKey. Consume `accessTokenParsed.data` consistently and drop the unreachable success check.

The webhook secret is compared with a plain `!==` string comparison, which is not constant-time and leaks the secret through response timing; an attacker able to hit this public webhook endpoint can recover the shared secret byte-by-byte. Compare with a constant-time function (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers).

`symmetricDecrypt` throws on a malformed ciphertext (crypto createDecipheriv / final) and `JSON.parse` throws on non-JSON decrypted content, so a webhook body with a bad `keys` value produces an unhandled 500 rather than a 4xx. Wrap the decrypt/parse in a try/catch and return a validation error response.

The findFirst-then-create sequence is a check-then-act with no unique constraint or lock, so two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user+app both see no credential and both insert, producing duplicate credentials that then conflict on downstream reads. Use an upsert keyed on (userId, appId) or add a unique constraint and handle the conflict.

When `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is configured, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw fetch `Response` object, but the zoho-bigin (`CalendarService.ts:96-115`), zohocrm (`CalendarService.ts:217-236`) and hubspot (`CalendarService.ts:177-202`) callers consume the result as an axios/typed object (`tokenInfo.data.error`, `hubspotRefreshToken.expiryDate`). A fetch `Response` has no `.data`, so `tokenInfo.data` is `undefined` and the first property access throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`, breaking every token refresh in these apps when credential sync is enabled. Return the parsed token payload (e.g. `await response.json()`) or make callers branch on the sync path so the returned shape matches what each caller expects.

issues.descricao: The new app-credential webhook checks its shared secret with a plain !== string comparison instead of a constant-time comparison, leaking timing information about the secret.

comentarios.texto: Direct !== comparison of webhook secret leaks via timing attack. Use constant-time comparison (e.g., crypto.timingSafeEqual on hashed/buffered values with length check) instead of `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`.

The webhook authenticates a secret using direct string inequality, which is not constant-time and can leak information about the secret through comparison timing. Compare fixed-length representations using a constant-time primitive (such as crypto.timingSafeEqual), handling absent or malformed headers safely, instead of comparing the secret strings directly.

The webhook secret is compared with the `!==` operator, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and leaks the secret via response timing (timing attack). An attacker can iteratively recover CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET and then forge requests that create/update arbitrary user credential keys (decrypted with the AES key) via this endpoint. Use a constant-time comparison, e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers, guarding for length mismatch first.

issues.descricao: The webhook parses the body with zod .parse and decrypts/JSON-parses the keys without error handling, so invalid payloads produce 500 errors instead of 400 responses.
issues.textoGolden: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: zod parse, symmetricDecrypt and JSON.parse throw unhandled (no try/catch) with no method guard. WHY: Invalid body/keys or GET request crashes handler with 500 and leaks stack, instead of 400/405. HOW: Wrap parse/decrypt in try/catch returning 400 and restrict to POST.

schema .parse plus symmetricDecrypt/JSON.parse throw unhandled (ZodError, decrypt error, SyntaxError) on invalid body or tampered keys, crashing webhook with 500. Use safeParse and try/catch with 400 responses.

issues.descricao: The webhook's non-atomic findFirst-then-create lets concurrent deliveries for the same user and app insert duplicate credential rows.

comentarios.texto: The webhook performs a non-atomic findFirst followed by create when no credential exists. Concurrent deliveries for the same user and app can both observe no row and insert duplicates because Credential has no unique userId/appId constraint; subsequent findFirst updates only one duplicate, leaving competing credentials stale. Serialize the lookup/create operation for each user/app pair or introduce an appropriate uniqueness constraint and atomic upsert.

issues.descricao: parseRefreshTokenResponse writes the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when the refresh response omits a refresh token, so the stored credential gets an invalid refresh token and later refreshes fail.
issues.textoGolden: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

comentarios.texto: The parser fabricates the literal refresh token "refresh_token" whenever a successful response omits refresh_token, including when synchronization is disabled. Office365's response schema explicitly permits that omission, and its caller merges parsed data over existing credentials, replacing the valid saved refresh token with this invalid value and breaking the next refresh. Leave the property absent so the existing token survives the merge.

When a refresh response omits refresh_token, this helper manufactures the hardcoded credential "refresh_token". Callers such as Office365 merge this into stored credentials, overwriting the valid existing refresh token and causing subsequent provider refreshes to use a predictable invalid token. Leave the field absent and preserve the existing credential when omission is allowed by the provider, or reject the response when a refresh token is required; do not substitute a literal authentication token.

WHAT: Missing refresh_token is replaced with literal string "refresh_token". WHY: Stores bogus refresh token in DB, breaking all future refreshes and masking provider errors. HOW: Preserve existing credential refresh_token or throw instead of injecting placeholder.

issues.descricao: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed keys from z.string().toString(), which produce a literal key rather than a wildcard, so the sync-mode schema does not validate or keep expiry and other token fields as intended.
issues.textoGolden: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

comentarios.texto: `[z.string().toString()]` evaluates to a fixed string key such as "ZodString", so minimumTokenResponseSchema requires a literal numeric property with that name. Every synced token response fails validation and throws "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Use `z.object({access_token: z.string()}).passthrough()` instead.

The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` evaluate to the literal string "[object Object]", not a wildcard. The schema therefore requires a numeric property named "[object Object]", so safeParse always fails in credential-sync mode and the function throws "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Use `.passthrough()` on an object with access_token and optional numeric expiry fields instead.

The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` evaluate to a literal string like "ZodString" and not to a wildcard. The schema therefore requires a numeric property with that nonsense name and never matches real token responses. In sync mode every refresh throws "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". Use `.passthrough()` and a real expiry check instead.

issues.descricao: In sync mode refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response, but callers expect their provider-specific shapes (res.data, axios .data, HubspotToken), so token refresh breaks for Google, Zoho and HubSpot when credential sharing is on.
issues.textoGolden: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

comentarios.texto:
WHAT: In the credential-sharing branch `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response` object instead of a parsed token payload, yet several callers treat the result as an already-parsed token object.
WHY: Callers such as hubspot (`hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn`), zoho-bigin (`tokenInfo.data.error`), zohocrm (`zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error`) and googlecalendar (`res?.data`) read `.data`/token fields off the return value; a `Response` has neither, so the sync path yields `undefined`/`NaN` or throws a TypeError — the feature's primary code path is broken for those apps.
HOW: Parse the response (e.g. `const data = await response.json(); return data;`) before returning, or make every caller await the appropriate response handler.

In sharing mode refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch Response (no `.data`), but the google caller reads `res?.data` and then `token.access_token`, throwing a TypeError swallowed by the catch, so the token is never refreshed.

`res?.data` assumes the value returned by refreshOAuthTokens has a `.data` field (true for the `fetchTokens.res` branch), but when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED the helper returns a raw `fetch()` Response, which has no `.data`. Then `token.access_token` throws. Either parse the shared-mode Response here or have refreshOAuthTokens return a normalized `{ data }` shape.

issues.descricao: Google Calendar persists the safeParse result object instead of its data as the credential key, corrupting the stored credential so later reads fail.
issues.textoGolden: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

comentarios.texto: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a SafeParse result {success,data}, not the parsed key. Storing it directly as `key` writes the wrapper to the credential. Unwrap like other callers: check .success and use .data.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns SafeParse result {success,data}, but call site stores that wrapper as credential `key` (previously googleCredentialSchema.parse() returned the plain object). Store `key.data` / handle wrapper, otherwise persisted credential becomes {success,data} shape and subsequent credential reads fail.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns SafeParse wrapper {success,data} but code stores the whole wrapper as credential.key. Office365calendar in same PR unwraps via .data. Persisted credential will be {success,data} instead of tokens, so next load fails validation. Unwrap to .data after success check.

issues.descricao: After switching to parseRefreshTokenResponse, the tokenResponse.success check in Office365 refreshAccessToken is dead code and the previous error logging was dropped.

comentarios.texto: parseRefreshTokenResponse now throws when parsing fails, so the `tokenResponse.success` check on the next line is dead code and the previous error logging was removed. A failed refresh now throws out of refreshAccessToken instead of keeping the old credentials. Catch the error or restore the previous handling.

issues.descricao: Salesforce getClient now refreshes the OAuth token and writes the credential on every service construction, adding a network round trip and DB write even when the access token is valid.

comentarios.texto: getClient now unconditionally exchanges the Salesforce refresh token on every service construction, even when the saved access token is valid. Each constructor invocation adds a blocking OAuth network round trip and credential database write before any Salesforce operation, replacing jsforce's existing on-demand refresh behavior. Keep refresh on demand or guard the exchange with a token-expiration check.

issues.descricao: The new Salesforce token refresh uses prisma without importing it, so the code fails type checking and throws a ReferenceError at runtime.

comentarios.texto: The new credential update references prisma without importing or declaring it; searching this file finds only the new usage. This fails TypeScript checking and raises ReferenceError after a successful token exchange at runtime. Import prisma from @calcom/prisma before using it.

issues.descricao: Zoho Bigin passes the credential id instead of the user id to refreshOAuthTokens, so the sync endpoint receives the wrong calcomUserId.
issues.textoGolden: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

comentarios.texto:
WHAT: The 3rd argument to `refreshOAuthTokens` is `credentialId` (= `credential.id`, line 53), but the function's parameter is `userId` (`refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFunction, appSlug, userId)`).
WHY: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED, the sync endpoint is sent `calcomUserId: <credential id>` instead of the user id, so Bigin credentials are synced against the wrong/non-existent user (all other apps correctly pass `credential.userId`).
HOW: Pass `credential.userId` instead of `credentialId` as the third argument.

refreshOAuthTokens' third parameter is the Cal.com userId (used as `calcomUserId` in the sync request and to decide whether sharing runs), but this call passes `credentialId`. Every other caller passes `credential.userId`, so the credential-sync endpoint receives a credential row id as the user id and shared credentials are fetched/updated for the wrong identity. Pass `credential.userId` here.

refreshOAuthTokens' third parameter is `userId` (declared in refreshOAuthTokens.ts line 3 and used as `calcomUserId: userId.toString()`), but this call passes `credentialId` (the Credential row id, line 53) instead of the user id. When credential sharing is enabled the customer's sync endpoint receives a credential id labelled as calcomUserId and cannot resolve the correct Cal.com user. Pass `credential.userId` (the BiginToken/credential payload carries it) or plumb the user id through refreshAccessToken.

issues.descricao: Salesforce checks response.statusText !== 'OK' instead of response.ok when refreshing the token, which can misclassify successful responses, and then ignores the refreshed token.
issues.textoGolden: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Checks response.statusText !== "OK" instead of response.ok and builds jsforce.Connection from stale credentialKey.access_token/instance_url ignoring accessTokenParsed.data. WHY: Refresh never takes effect (old token reused) and valid refreshes can throw on runtimes where statusText is empty. HOW: Check !response.ok and use parsed access_token/instance_url for connection and DB update.

issues.descricao: After refreshing the Salesforce token, jsforce.Connection is created with the stale access_token and instance_url instead of the newly refreshed values.
issues.textoGolden: The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

comentarios.texto:
WHAT: The new block fetches and persists a fresh access token (`accessTokenParsed.data`) but then creates the `jsforce.Connection` with the stale `credentialKey.access_token` (line 106) instead of the just-refreshed token.
WHY: The refreshed token is written to the DB but never used for the connection; if the old token was expired, jsforce must refresh again (extra round trip) or fail, and the DB/connection state diverge.
HOW: Pass the new access token (`accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`) to the `jsforce.Connection`.

issues.descricao: The app-credential webhook looks up appStoreMetadata by app.slug, but the map is keyed by dirName, so apps whose slug differs from their directory (e.g. google-calendar) always get a 404 and their credentials cannot be synced.

sugestoes.texto: The `before_validation` callback calls `self.host.sub!(...)` without guarding for a nil host. When the admin controller assigns a blank/missing `params[:embeddable_host][:host]`, `self.host` is nil and `nil.sub!` raises NoMethodError, turning an intended validation error into a crash instead of returning `render_json_error`. Guard with a presence check (e.g. `if self.host.present?`) before mutating.

`execute("...INNER JOIN site_settings...")[0]['id']` dereferences `[0]` which is nil whenever the `embed_category` setting row is missing or its value matches no category name, so `nil['id']` raises NoMethodError and aborts the migration. Fetch the row and check for presence before reading `['id']` (and integer-cast defensively).

Host values from the old `embeddable_hosts` setting are interpolated directly into the INSERT statement (`VALUES ('#{h}', ...)`). A hostname containing a single quote — including any previously stored setting value — breaks the SQL and aborts the migration. Escape the value or use ActiveRecord `EmbeddableHost.create!` / bound parameters instead of string interpolation.

The `update` action never reads `params` or persists anything; it only re-serializes `@embedding` and returns success, so the frontend `saveChanges` action (`embedding.update({})`) silently loses changes while reporting success. Either implement the intended persistence or remove the endpoint/route so the client does not assume the save succeeded.

`update` and `destroy` fetch the record with `EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first`, which returns nil for an unknown or already-deleted id. In `destroy` the following `host.destroy` and in `update` the delegated `host.host = ...` both raise NoMethodError on nil, returning a 500 instead of a clean 404. Guard with a presence check (render json: not_found / return) before operating on the record.

Host values read from the legacy `embeddable_hosts` site setting are interpolated directly into the INSERT SQL (`VALUES ('#{h}', ...)`) without escaping. Any single quote or SQL fragment in that admin-set value breaks out of the string literal and is executed as SQL during the migration. Use parameterized inserts (bind host/category_id) or the model/ActiveRecord API instead of string interpolation.

issues.descricao: EmbeddableHost's before_validation calls self.host.sub! unconditionally, so saving a record with a nil host raises NoMethodError instead of returning a validation error.
issues.textoGolden: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.

comentarios.texto: The before_validation callback calls `sub!` on host without guarding nil. Creating a host with a missing or null host field reaches this callback from save_host and raises NoMethodError instead of returning a validation error. Guard nil during normalization and let presence/format validation reject it.

WHAT: `before_validation` calls `self.host.sub!(...)` unconditionally, so a record with a nil host raises NoMethodError (`nil.sub!`) instead of producing a normal format-invalid result. WHY: `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController#save_host` assigns `params[:embeddable_host][:host]` directly; any request that omits the host value makes the save raise a 500 instead of returning the `render_json_error(host)` validation response. HOW: guard the mutation, e.g. `return if host.blank?` at the top of the before_validation block (or use `self.host = self.host.to_s` before stripping).

before_validation calls self.host.sub!(...) on a possibly-nil host before validates_format_of runs. The controller assigns host.host = params[:embeddable_host][:host], so a request without a host key leaves it nil and nil.sub! raises NoMethodError at save time instead of the format validation producing a normal error response. Add a presence guard so validation reports the failure.

issues.descricao: update and destroy in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController fetch the host with where(id:).first and never check for nil, so an unknown id raises NoMethodError and returns a 500 instead of not-found.
issues.textoGolden: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.

comentarios.texto: In the destroy action, the nil-host case (line 15-16) would raise NoMethodError. Consider adding a nil check to handle the case where the host is not found.

update and destroy fetch the record with EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first but never check for nil, then immediately use it (save_host(host) does host.host = ... / host.save; destroy does host.destroy). A stale or already-deleted id, or an interleaving where a concurrent delete removes the row first, makes host nil and the first call on it raises NoMethodError -> unhandled 500. Guard with a nil/404 check before use.

Update passes the nullable result of where(...).first directly to save_host, which immediately assigns host.host. Updating a nonexistent or concurrently deleted record returns an internal error instead of a not-found response; destroy has the same lookup failure. Use find or explicitly raise a not-found error before dereferencing the lookup result.

issues.descricao: record_for_host compares lower(host) against the un-lowercased URI host, so mixed-case referer hosts fail to match allowed hosts and embedding is rejected.
issues.textoGolden: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

comentarios.texto: Normalize the parsed hostname before comparing it with lower(host). URI parsing preserves hostname case, so an allowed entry such as example.com does not match https://EXAMPLE.com/page even though DNS hostnames are case-insensitive. This makes valid embedding requests fail the host authorization check and makes category lookup inconsistent for equivalent domain identities. Compare against host.downcase (or normalize both operands equivalently), and add a mixed-case URL test.

The query compares lower(host) to the un-downcased uri.host. A referer such as http://EvilTrout.com never matches the stored lowercase host, so embedding is wrongly denied. Fix: use where("lower(host) = ?", host.downcase).

The query compares lower(host) in the database with uri.host, which is not lowercased, so the comparison normalizes only one side. A referer or URL with uppercase letters (e.g. http://EvilTrout.com) will not match the stored host. Compare against host.downcase, i.e. where('lower(host) = ?', host.downcase).

issues.descricao: The migration copies the legacy embeddable_hosts values into the new table without stripping scheme and path, so hosts stored as http://example.com no longer match the bare-host lookup and previously allowed embeds are rejected after upgrade.
issues.textoGolden: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: migration inserts raw embeddable_hosts lines (e.g. http://example.com/123) without stripping scheme/path like the model does. WHY: migrated rows never match EmbeddableHost.record_for_host which compares bare uri.host, silently breaking previously allowed embeds.

Migration INSERTs raw embeddable_hosts lines with scheme/path intact, but EmbeddableHost normalizes to bare domain (before_validation strips protocol/path, record_for_host looks up by URI.host). Strip protocol and path before INSERT or migrated hosts will never satisfy host_allowed?.

Legacy hosts are inserted verbatim instead of applying the new model's scheme/path normalization. Existing values such as http://discourse.org or https://example.com/1234 remain in the table, while record_for_host compares only URI.host, so previously configured embedding hosts stop working after upgrade. Normalize migrated entries to the same representation used by the model before inserting them.

issues.descricao: The contents of category_fabricator.rb and embeddable_host_fabricator.rb are swapped, so each file defines the other's fabricators.
issues.textoGolden: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.

comentarios.texto: File named category_fabricator.rb now defines Fabricator(:embeddable_host) while Fabricator(:category) was moved to embeddable_host_fabricator.rb. Filenames disagree with contents — swap contents back so each file defines the fabricator its name states.

The file names and contents are swapped. embeddable_host_fabricator.rb defines the category fabricators (:category, :diff_category, :happy_category, :private_category), and category_fabricator.rb defines :embeddable_host. Restore category_fabricator.rb to the original category fabricators and put the :embeddable_host fabricator in embeddable_host_fabricator.rb.

issues.descricao: The migration builds its INSERT by interpolating each legacy host value into the SQL string instead of quoting or binding it, so a value with a quote breaks the statement.
issues.textoGolden: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.

comentarios.texto: The migration's INSERT statement uses string interpolation: VALUES ('#{h}', ...). This is a SQL-injection concern and should be fixed by using parameterized queries or proper escaping.
WHAT: migration interpolates raw host string into SQL: VALUES ('#{h}', ...). WHY: a host value containing a single quote breaks the statement and allows SQL injection via site_settings value.

issues.descricao: The migration reads execute(...)[0]['id'] for embed_category without checking for an empty result, so installs without that setting stored crash the migration instead of falling back to the uncategorized category.
issues.textoGolden: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: migration does execute(...)[0]['id'] with no guard when embed_category setting/category is missing. WHY: nil[0] dereference crashes the migration and blocks deploy on instances without that setting.
Migration does execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking empty result; missing site_settings row throws NoMethodError and fails migration. Check for nil row.

The migration indexes the first category-query result before checking whether any row was returned. An installation without a persisted embed_category setting, or with no matching category name, aborts migration before reaching the uncategorized fallback. Check whether the result contains a row before accessing its id and handle missing fallback settings as well.

issues.descricao: The spec 'is false if embeddable_host is blank' no longer sets up any host condition and passes only because embed_truncate defaults to false, so its name no longer matches what it tests.

comentarios.texto: Test 'is false if embeddable_host is blank' does not establish the true-branch preconditions (embed_truncate true, has_topic_embed true) nor control host presence, so it passes regardless of host logic and would still pass if host checking were broken/removed. Set truncate true + stub embed true with no hosts for the false case.

The test named "is false if embeddable_host is blank" now uses an ordinary built topic without setting embed_truncate or making has_topic_embed? true. It therefore returns false for reasons unrelated to the missing host, and passes even with the new implementation that never checks host availability. If blank-host behavior remains the intended contract, arrange all the other prerequisites before asserting false; if the contract intentionally changed, replace this case with a test of the actual intended behavior rather than retaining a misleading passing test.

The description "is false if embeddable_host is blank" no longer matches the code. This PR changed Topic#expandable_first_post? (app/models/topic.rb:869) to `SiteSetting.embed_truncate? && has_topic_embed?`, removing the embeddable_hosts condition entirely, and removed the `SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts` setup from this test. The assertion now passes only because `has_topic_embed?` is unstubbed (false) and embed_truncate is unset, so the name states a cause the method no longer has — rename it (e.g. "is false when there is no topic embed") or set up the precondition it claims to test.

issues.descricao: The 'find embedded' test requests fruit 2 but the pretender always returns fruit 1, so it asserts fruit 1's colors and would not notice a find that ignores the id.

comentarios.texto: Test requests fruit id 2 but pretender returns fruits[0] unconditionally, so assertions on colors [1,2] never cover fruit 2's color_ids [3]. Make pretender honor :id or request id 1 / assert single-element case to actually verify plural _ids hydration.

This test now requests fruit 2 but expects fruit 1's two colors. The /fruits/:id Pretender handler always returns fruits[0], so the test passes while hydrating the wrong record and would not catch a find implementation that ignores the requested ID. Make the handler select the requested fruit and assert its ID and corresponding colors (fruit 2 has only color 3), or request fruit 1 if testing its two-color hydration is the goal.

issues.descricao: After saving a host, the component overwrites its category with findById(categoryId); when no category was chosen this is null even though the server saved the uncategorized category, so the row shows no category until reload.

comentarios.texto: The save callback overwrites the category using categoryId even when the server substituted the uncategorized category for a blank selection. Adding a host without choosing a category therefore leaves its category badge empty, and editing it reads an undefined category id despite a valid category_id having been returned. Resolve the category from the saved response's category_id rather than the submitted selection.

When categoryId is null (the default for a new row, or a cleared selection), the controller saves SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id and returns that category_id. This callback instead overwrites host.category with findById(null), making the displayed category disagree with the saved category. Use the category from the save response or its returned category_id rather than the pre-save selection.

Use the saved response's category rather than overwriting it from categoryId after saving. For a new host with no category selected, categoryId is null, while the new controller deliberately saves SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id and returns that ID through the serializer. This callback replaces the hydrated category with findById(null), leaving the row without its actual category until reload (and reopening edit also initializes from that incorrect relationship).

issues.descricao: Hosts saved with a port (allowed by the validation regex) are stored as host:port, but lookup compares only URI.host, so those configured hosts never match and embedding fails for them.

comentarios.texto: Host lookup compares URI.host against a stored value that validation explicitly permits to include a port. Saving example.com:8080 succeeds, but a request from http://example.com:8080 produces URI.host equal to example.com and never matches that record, disabling embedding and retrieval for the configured host. Use a consistent port representation in both storage and lookup.

The validator accepts hosts such as `example.com:8080`, but record_for_host extracts only URI.host (`example.com`) and compares it to the stored port-qualified string. An accepted and saved host therefore never authorizes its corresponding URLs. Normalize the stored and queried authority consistently, including a deliberate port policy.

issues.descricao: EmbeddableHost's host format validation only accepts TLDs of 2-5 letters, so admins cannot add embeddable hosts on longer TLDs like example.technology.
record_for_host queries lower(host) on embeddable_hosts, which has no index on host.
The describe block is named allows_embeddable_host but tests host_allowed?.

sugestoes.texto: `updateDevice` treats `rowsAffected == 0` as `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, but `RowsAffected()` reports rows *changed*, not rows matched: Postgres (and MySQL without CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS) returns 0 when the UPDATE matches the row but writes identical values. Because `TagDevice` sets `UpdatedAt: time.Now()` (impl.go:141) and the column has microsecond precision on Postgres, a repeat tag for an existing device whose timestamp lands in the same microsecond yields 0 changed rows, so a *valid, already-registered* device is rejected as "device limit reached" and `Authenticate` (client.go:45-47) returns an error that blocks anonymous authentication for that user. Either match on existence instead of rows-changed (e.g. SELECT the row first, or distinguish the no-op case) so that a legitimate device update is not misreported as a limit violation, or return a distinct error for "device not found" versus "limit reached".

`ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` swapped the injected `anonStore anonstore.AnonStore` for `sqlStore db.DB` and now constructs the concrete store inline (`anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore(sqlStore, cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit)`), so any caller or test that injected a custom/mock `AnonStore` is silently bypassed, and the separate wire provider `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` still registered at `pkg/server/wire.go:374` now requires an `int64` argument that no wire binding or provider supplies — the generated wire code must be regenerated or the build/startup fails with an unresolved `int64` dependency. Either remove the standalone `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` wire entry, or keep accepting an `AnonStore` and pass the device limit through that seam, so the wiring stays resolvable and mock stores remain injectable.

Every `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call on the anonymous-auth hot path now runs an extra `CountDevices` aggregate over the whole `anon_device` table for the 30-day window before performing the write, doubling DB round-trips per tagged anonymous request (one COUNT + one INSERT/UPDATE instead of one write). With a high anonymous request rate this COUNT runs on every request and, absent an index on `updated_at` over that range, forces a scan of the device table; consider caching the count for a short interval or checking the limit only when the row is not already known to exist (e.g. on INSERT conflict) instead of on every tag.

The new updateDevice closure mutates the outer `args` slice via `args = append([]interface{}{query}, args...)`, so each retry of the same callback prepends `query` again. Because WithDbSession retries the callback on sqlite ErrLocked/ErrBusy (session.go:127 -> retryer.Retry), a retried execution passes a corrupted argument list (`Exec(query, query, ...)`) with a placeholder/value count mismatch, turning the update into an error. Build the argument list inside the closure (e.g. `qArgs := append([]interface{}{query}, device.ClientIP, device.UserAgent, ...)`) so it is not mutated across invocations.

issues.descricao: The device limit check counts devices and then inserts in separate non-atomic steps, so concurrent requests from new devices can all pass the check and exceed the configured limit.
issues.textoGolden: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.

comentarios.texto: The limit check counts devices and then inserts in separate steps with no lock or transaction. Concurrent requests from new devices can all see count < limit and all insert, so the limit is exceeded. Make the count-and-insert atomic, for example with a conditional INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*)) < limit.

The device limit check is a non-atomic count followed by an insert. Concurrent requests from different new devices can all see count < limit and all insert, so the number of devices exceeds deviceLimit. Make the check and insert atomic, for example with a conditional INSERT ... SELECT WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*)) < limit, or serialize the check and insert under a lock.

WHAT: CreateOrUpdateDevice does check-then-act (CountDevices then INSERT/UPSERT) with no lock, transaction, or unique-guard when deviceLimit>0. WHY: Two concurrent new-device requests can both observe count < limit and both insert, exceeding the configured limit and breaking the enforcement contract. HOW: Enforce atomically (e.g., conditional insert guarded by count in one statement/transaction with serializable lock, or re-check count on conflict).

issues.descricao: Device slots are keyed by the client-controlled X-Grafana-Device-Id header with no validation or rate limiting, so an anonymous caller can fill the limit with fake IDs and deny anonymous access to every new legitimate device.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Device slots counted toward deviceLimit are keyed by the unauthenticated X-Grafana-Device-Id header (read in impl.go TagDevice) with no validation or rate-limit. WHY: Any anonymous caller can mint arbitrary device IDs to fill the table up to the limit, after which all legitimate new anonymous devices get ErrDeviceLimitReached and authentication is denied — a trivial anonymous-access DoS introduced by the limit. HOW: Do not let a single client consume many slots (e.g., bind slot consumption to IP/fingerprint, rate-limit new-device creation, or require proof of distinct device).

issues.descricao: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a new device is rejected at the limit and never verifies that an existing device can still be updated at the limit.

comentarios.texto: The at-limit call reuses a brand-new device ID ("keep") that was never inserted, so it only reaches updateDevice's `rowsAffected == 0` -> ErrDeviceLimitReached branch. The success branch of the newly added updateDevice (an existing device still being updated while the store is at the limit) is never exercised by any test — every other call uses deviceLimit 0, so updateDevice is never invoked. A regression that made updateDevice always affect 0 rows, use a wrong WHERE/SET, or unconditionally return ErrDeviceLimitReached whenever limit>0 would leave this and all other tests green. Add a case that, after the store is at the limit, calls CreateOrUpdateDevice again with the SAME DeviceID and asserts require.NoError (and ideally that client_ip/user_agent/updated_at were changed), so the update path is actually verified.

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a new device is rejected at the limit. It would still pass if updateDevice always returned ErrDeviceLimitReached, because it never re-submits the existing device (DeviceID "32mdo31deeqwes") at the limit. Add a call that updates the existing device with a new UserAgent or UpdatedAt, require NoError, and check the stored row changed.

issues.descricao: tagDeviceUI caches the device key before CreateOrUpdateDevice; when the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached the entry stays, so the next request from the same device skips the limit check and authenticates for up to 29 minutes.
issues.textoGolden: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: TagDevice failures that triggered the new ErrDeviceLimitReached early-return are not permanent, because tagDeviceUI (impl.go:87) writes the device key into localCache BEFORE CreateOrUpdateDevice (impl.go:93) and never evicts it on error; tagDeviceUI returns early on any cache hit (impl.go:83-84). WHY: the first request from a new over-limit device is denied, but the poisoned cache makes every subsequent request from that same device skip the limit check entirely and authenticate successfully, so the configurable device limit is bypassed by simply retrying. HOW: only set the cache key after CreateOrUpdateDevice returns nil (e.g. move a.localCache.SetDefault after the successful DB write, or delete the key when it returns ErrDeviceLimitReached).

TagDevice now propagates ErrDeviceLimitReached to deny an over-limit anonymous device, but tagDeviceUI (impl.go:83-95) records the device in localCache at line 87 *before* calling a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the store rejects the device with ErrDeviceLimitReached, the key is already cached, so the next request for that same device returns early at line 83 with a nil error and the device is admitted. The limit therefore only blocks the first request and is silently bypassed on retry. Fix by only setting the cache entry after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds (move SetDefault after the store call), or by removing/not caching the key on failure.

The new authentication gate accepts retries from devices that were rejected by the limit because tagDeviceUI inserts the cache entry before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds. At capacity, the first request with a new X-Grafana-Device-Id fails, but subsequent requests with that same ID hit the 29-minute cache and receive an anonymous identity without admission to the device store. Cache only successful admissions, and ensure concurrent requests cannot treat an in-progress admission as successful.

issues.descricao: Device tagging now runs synchronously in Authenticate, adding DB round-trips on cache-miss anonymous requests where it used to be fire-and-forget.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Anonymous.Authenticate changed from fire-and-forget goroutine TagDevice to synchronous TagDevice(ctx) that runs CountDevices + INSERT/UPDATE inline. WHY: Every cache-miss anonymous authentication now blocks on two DB round-trips in the login hot path, adding latency and DB load per request where previously auth returned immediately. HOW: Restore async tagging for the non-limit path or at least decouple denial from the hot path (e.g., async count with cached count, or only synchronously enforce when near limit).

issues.descricao: The new auth.anonymous device_limit setting has no entry in conf/defaults.ini, so the GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_DEVICE_LIMIT environment override is ignored and the limit stays 0.

comentarios.texto: The new device_limit setting is read without adding a corresponding key to conf/defaults.ini. applyEnvVariableOverrides only visits keys already present in the loaded INI and runs before readAuthSettings, so setting GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_DEVICE_LIMIT alone is ignored and leaves the limit at zero, disabling enforcement. Add an uncommented device_limit = 0 entry under auth.anonymous in defaults.ini so the standard environment override mechanism can apply it.

issues.descricao: The anonymous device limit is enforced only through TagDevice, which returns nil when the client-controlled device ID header is missing, so requests without the header authenticate anonymously regardless of the configured limit.

The doc comment on updateDevice says it updates a device "updated between the given times", but the function takes no times, computes the 30-day window itself and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when no row matches.
updateDevice prepends the query to the captured args inside the retried DB callback, so a SQLite lock retry runs Exec with the query duplicated in the arguments and the update fails.

sugestoes.texto: The listener is gated on Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1), but the V2 permissions classes are selected via Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2, which is an independent feature (Profile.java lines 56/58) and the only one enabled in the V2 test/realm configs. Under a V2-only deployment this guard evaluates false, so the RoleRemovedEvent/ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent branches (including the newly added client branch) never run and the setPermissionsEnabled(..., false) cleanup is silently skipped, leaving stale permission resources after a client/role/group removal. Gate the listener on the V2 feature as well (e.g. check ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ || ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2), or remove the guard since it had none before this change.

When the client has no per-client resource, `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE)` returns null whenever the all-"Clients" resource has not been provisioned yet, and the code then dereferences it: `findByResource(server, null)` and `new ResourcePermission(resource, resource.getScopes(), server)` will throw a NullPointerException instead of returning false. Add a null check after the fallback lookup and return false when the resource-type resource is absent.

getClientsWithPermission iterates every resource of type "Clients" and calls hasGrantedPermission for each, and hasGrantedPermission performs a full `root.evaluatePermission` per resource — one policy evaluation per client on every call. On realms with many clients this is an O(N) authorization fan-out in a listing path; load the resource-type resource's permissions once, or batch the evaluation, instead of evaluating per client resource.

issues.descricao: Claims the removal-cleanup listener is guarded by the V1 fine-grained flag, so client/role/group permissions are orphaned when V1 is disabled or only V2 is enabled.
issues.textoGolden: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

comentarios.texto: The cleanup is now entirely wrapped in Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ), so when the feature is disabled the pre-existing removal cleanup (roles/clients/groups .setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)) no longer runs. Realms using the non-V2 permission model will keep orphaned authorization resources/permissions after a client, role or group is removed. The gate should preserve the old behavior when the feature is off (run for V1), or the V1 cleanup must be performed elsewhere.

issues.descricao: getClientsWithPermission in ClientPermissionsV2 only finds the type-level 'Clients' resource and returns its name, never actual client ids, so callers that resolve the returned values as client ids get wrong results or null clients.
issues.textoGolden: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

issues.descricao: Claims getResourceTypeResource can return null in ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, causing a NullPointerException in findByResource.
issues.textoGolden: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.

issues.descricao: ClientPermissionsV2 has an unused private getEvaluationContext method.
issues.textoGolden: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

comentarios.texto: Dead computation: `getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken)` is private and has no caller anywhere in the class. Its only possible consumer in the V1 class, `canExchangeTo`, was overridden to throw UnsupportedOperationException (line 148-150). The EvaluationContext and its overridden getBaseAttributes are built and then never used — remove the method (or wire it into canExchangeTo if token-exchange is meant to be supported).

issues.descricao: The Javadoc of the void requireView() and requireViewClientScopes() methods says they return true instead of documenting that they throw ForbiddenException.

comentarios.texto: The Javadoc for `void requireView()` says "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}", but requireView() is void and throws ForbiddenException rather than returning a value. It is a copy-paste of the canView() doc and should read "Throws ForbiddenException if {@link #canView()} returns {@code false}", matching the sibling require* methods (requireListClientScopes, requireConfigure, etc.).

The Javadoc for `void requireViewClientScopes()` says "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}", but the method is void and throws ForbiddenException. The doc describes a boolean return the method never produces; it should state that it throws ForbiddenException if canViewClientScopes() returns false, consistent with the other require* methods.

Declaration does not match the method it documents: the javadoc for `requireView()` ('Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}.') and for `requireViewClientScopes()` ('Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}.') describes a boolean-returning accessor, but both methods are declared `void` and are the require* counterparts that throw ForbiddenException (as documented for requireManage/requireConfigure above). The text was copy-pasted from the corresponding can* methods; it should state that the method throws when canView()/canViewClientScopes() is false.

issues.descricao: ClientPermissionsV2.canView() ignores a global MANAGE permission, so admins with only global manage take the unpaginated, per-client evaluated listing path.

comentarios.texto: canView() does not recognize an all-clients MANAGE permission even though canView(client) grants viewing through canConfigure(client) and canManage(client). For an administrator with global MANAGE but no VIEW, ClientsResource.getClients selects an unpaginated realm-wide client stream and evaluates authorization for clients before applying pagination, instead of fetching the requested database page. Include the global MANAGE permission in the global viewing capability while preserving client-specific denial semantics.

issues.descricao: canView(client) short-circuits on the global all-clients VIEW permission, so a client-specific permission denying an admin is never evaluated and the client is still viewable.

comentarios.texto: The global VIEW check returns true before evaluating client-specific VIEW permissions, bypassing a negative permission on an individual client. An administrator granted VIEW on all clients can therefore read a client explicitly excluded by a client-specific denial; ClientsResource.getClients also bypasses per-client checks when this evaluator's parameterless canView() returns true. Evaluate the specific client resource before falling back to the all-clients permission, and ensure listing does not use a global grant to skip specific denials.

Do not short-circuit resource-specific view evaluation on the global fine-grained VIEW grant. With an all-clients VIEW permission allowing an administrator and a client-specific VIEW permission denying that administrator, canView() returns true here and the specific client permission is never evaluated. This differs from the specific-over-global override behavior exercised for users in this PR and exposes the denied client's representation. Keep the administrative-role bypass separate from fine-grained grants and evaluate the client's resource before falling back to the all-clients resource; also ensure the global view result used by client listing cannot bypass those overrides.

issues.descricao: The negative check for removing a default client scope expects ForbiddenException, but it can come from the preceding getDefaultClientScopes() call, so the test passes even without a permission check on removal.

comentarios.texto: The expected ForbiddenException can come from getDefaultClientScopes(), before removeDefaultClientScope() is invoked. With no permission granted, the initial read is forbidden, so this test still passes if removal's manage-permission check is removed entirely; the later granted removal also succeeds in that broken implementation. Obtain the scope ID using the privileged realm client outside this try block, then invoke only removeDefaultClientScope() through the restricted client and assert that it is forbidden.

issues.descricao: ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException, but AbstractTokenExchangeProvider still calls clients().canExchangeTo for client-to-client exchange, so with token exchange and FGAP V2 enabled the request fails with a server error instead of a permission decision.

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, an admin granted a permission on all clients is denied on any client that also has its own per-client permission resource, because only the per-client resource is evaluated.

sugestoes.texto: `safe_urlopen(...)` is invoked outside the `try` block that wraps only `safe_urlread(req)`, so a failed connection, SSL error, or timeout on the GitHub token endpoint raises an unhandled exception instead of routing to the error page. The equivalent code in `OAuth2CallbackView.exchange_token` (src/sentry/identity/oauth2.py:286-314) deliberately wraps the request itself and catches `SSLError`/`ConnectionError`; move `safe_urlopen` inside the `try` so transient GitHub/network failures degrade to the `error(...)` response rather than a 500.

`get_user_info` (src/sentry/identity/github/provider.py:7-17) calls `resp.raise_for_status()` and returns `resp.json()`, so a non-2xx response or a non-JSON body raises `HTTPError`/`JSONDecodeError`; this call is unguarded, unlike `OAuth2CallbackView` which catches those same failures, so a revoked/expired token or a GitHub hiccup aborts the installation with an unhandled exception instead of the generic verification-failure page. Wrap the `get_user_info` call and treat any exception as a verification failure (return `error(request, self.active_organization)`) before reading `authenticated_user_info["login"]`.

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` is indexed without checking that `sender` exists, but this key is only populated when the integration was created via the installation webhook (`build_integration` sets it only under `if state.get("sender")` at integration.py:376-377). An ACTIVE Integration created through the pipeline path lacks `sender`, so this raises `KeyError` and returns HTTP 500 instead of the intended `github-integration-failed.html` error page. Guard the lookup with `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` (and treat a missing sender as a failed verification), mirroring the existing `if "sender" not in integration.metadata` check in installation.py:44.

issues.descricao: error() calls _(error_short) on a variable and callers pass plain literals, so the short error strings are no longer extractable for translation.

comentarios.texto: The helper calls `_(error_short)` on a variable, and callers pass plain string literals. The translation extractor cannot see these strings, so the short error messages sent to the user are no longer translatable; the old code wrapped the literals directly in `_()`. Mark the literals with gettext_lazy at the call sites and the default, and pass them through without wrapping again.

error_short strings bypass translation extraction: _(error_short) uses a variable so makemessages cannot collect them. Wrap literals at definition/call sites, e.g. error_short=_("Invalid installation request.") and pass _("...") literals, then use data error value directly without re-wrapping.

Translate the short-message literals at their definition/call sites instead of calling `_(error_short)` on a variable. Django's message extraction cannot extract the default `"Invalid installation request."` or the plain-string arguments at the two call sites from this dynamic gettext invocation. The existing pending-deletion and already-installed messages previously appeared directly inside `_()`; this refactor removes their extraction sites, and the new default message cannot enter translation catalogs.
